_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Gemara. They are like consecrated property: and the prohibition of misuse [me’ila] applies to them.
rashi:a1.2: They are like non-sacred property: like the rest of the priest’s property.
rashi:a2.1: Granted, the Rabbis: of our mishna explain the reason, and [they explain] the verse of Rabbi Yehuda [ben Beteira], as it teaches: “If so, why is it stated: ‘Every dedicated item,’” and so on.
rashi:a3.1: Who consecrated his dedicated field: a field that an Israelite dedicated and that came into the portion of a priest. That he may not say: Since, when the Jubilee arrives, if I do not redeem it from the treasurer and another redeems it, it will be divided among the priests at the Jubilee, as is the law of one who consecrates an ancestral field (for a dedicated field is, for the priest, an ancestral field, as it is written: “As a field dedicated; its possession shall be to the priest”), then now that I hold it, let it be mine. For it is logical: with the property of others I acquire, since if an Israelite consecrated his ancestral field, when the Jubilee arrives it is divided to me; with my own, all the more so?
rashi:a4.1: The verse states: “As a field dedicated,” and so on: for this verse is written about one who consecrates an ancestral field.
rashi:a5.1: What have we learned from the dedicated field: about the ancestral field, and so on. Just as an ancestral field that an Israelite consecrated and one of the priests redeemed goes out of his hand at the Jubilee and is divided among all the members of the watch, as is said above in our chapter: “his ancestral possession,” his own, and this is not his own [25b], so too his dedicated field, and so on.
rashi:a8.1: He holds in accordance with Rabbi Yishmael: who derives it in the mishna [below] from “you shall consecrate” and “do not consecrate.”
rashi:a9.1: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: that unspecified dedications are for Temple maintenance.
rashi:a9.2: The baraita is taught the opposite way: that the Rabbis say [unspecified dedications are] for Temple maintenance, and Rabbi Yehuda [ben Beteira says they are] for the priests.
rashi:a10.1: Rav learned it by tradition: from his teacher; his teacher’s teacher taught him that the mishna is a corrupted text.
rashi:a11.1: And throw them: the four dinars, into the river, for they are consecrated to Temple maintenance. For if [the property were] for a priest, there would be no redemption for it, and it would have to be given to a priest.
rashi:a13.1: In the present time: when there is no Temple and there is no loss, but only a prohibition rests on them, even ab initio as well.
rashi:a15.1: A Hebrew slave is practiced only: that he is not sold in the present time.
rashi:a16.1: And an ancestral field does not [Rashi’s text reads “ancestral field”; the printed Gemara reads “dedicated field”]: the law of an ancestral field, that it is redeemed with a deduction [for the years the buyer has had it, does not apply]. Rather, if the buyer wishes to return it to him for whatever money he wishes, he returns it, and if not, one does not compel him. And likewise the law of one who consecrates an ancestral field at a time when the Temple stands but the Jubilee is not in force, such as after the tribes of Reuben and Gad were exiled, when the Jubilees ceased: it is redeemed only at its value.
rashi:a16.2: Houses of walled cities are not practiced: for we do not compel the buyer if the seller comes to redeem it, even within the year.
rashi:a17.1: A ger toshav is not practiced: [in the sense] that a Jew is commanded to sustain him. A ger toshav is one who accepted upon himself not to worship idols, and who eats carcasses [i.e., meat not slaughtered according to halakha].
rashi:a18.1: It is written: of a Hebrew slave, “Because he fares well with you,” and it is written of a ger toshav: “He shall dwell with you,” and so on. For “You shall not deliver a slave to his master” speaks of a ger toshav, as we establish it in tractate Gittin, in the chapter HaSholeiaḥ Get (45a), and after it is written: “He shall dwell with you, in your midst,” and so on. In any case, it is difficult for both of them [Rav Yehuda and Ulla], since it teaches: The [law of a] dedicated field is practiced only at a time when the Jubilee is in force.
rashi:a19.1: Land: is not practiced, as it is written: “When it goes out in the Jubilee… as a field dedicated.”
rashi:a20.1: Mishna. One verse says “you shall consecrate”: regarding a firstborn, as it is written: “All the firstborn [and so on] you shall consecrate” (Deuteronomy 15).
rashi:a20.2: And one verse says “shall not consecrate”: “However, the firstborn among animals that is born first to the Lord, a man shall not consecrate it,” and so on (Leviticus 27:26).
rashi:a21.1: A consecration of value: to raise it in monetary value, and he gives its benefit of discretion to the priest [i.e., what is consecrated is the money value of the owner’s right to choose the priest, as in the mishna on 28b].
rashi:a21.2: And you cannot consecrate it as a consecration for the altar: that the name of another offering should take effect on it.
rashi:a22.1: Gemara. And the Rabbis: who derive that exposition (above, 28b) from “Every dedicated item is most sacred.”
rashi:a22.2: “Do not consecrate” is needed for a prohibition: that if he designates it for the sake of another offering, he transgresses a prohibition.
rashi:a22.3: That it is a mitzva to consecrate it: for the sake of a firstborn, even though it is sacred on its own.
rashi:a23.1: And Rabbi Yishmael: says to you: If he does not consecrate it, is it not consecrated? [Said] in astonishment.
rashi:a23.2: He does not need to consecrate it: and Rabbi Yishmael does not accept this exposition.
tosafot:a11.1: Take four dinars and desacralize [the property] onto them, and throw them into the river, and it will be permitted to you: And if you say: But it says in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (13a): One does not consecrate, dedicate or pledge valuations in the present time, and if one consecrated, dedicated or pledged a valuation, an animal is hamstrung, and produce and vessels are left to rot. And here it is speaking of the present time, as it concludes here; so why do we not say they are left to rot? One must say that it says they are left to rot specifically of movable property, which does not lead to a stumbling block [i.e., misuse] if one waits until it rots. But here it is speaking of land, where, if one waits, it leads to a stumbling block. And so too it is found shortly after, where it says: “But that incident in Pumbedita was land.”
tosafot:a21.1: A consecration of value: meaning, to raise it in monetary value, to give the benefit of discretion to the priest.
gershom:a1.1: They are like consecrated property in every respect: that they are forbidden for benefit, and the prohibition of misuse applies to them.
gershom:a2.1: “Shall be yours”: even to betroth a woman with them, and the prohibition of misuse does not apply to them.
gershom:a3.1: [Granted, the Rabbis: who say [unspecified dedications are] for the priest, as they explain their reason, their own verse, and the verse of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, for an exposition.]
gershom:a4.1: But according to Rabbi Yehuda, what does “As a field dedicated” come for? And it cannot be established as referring to priests’ dedications, as [the Rabbis] explain it, for [according to him] that is derived from “Everything dedicated… shall be yours.”
gershom:a5.1: “As a field dedicated; its possession shall be to the priest”: why does the verse state it? Let it say “sacred to the Lord” and “it shall be to the priest”; why does the verse state “a dedicated field” (and “his possession”)?
gershom:a6.1: [His dedicated field: a field that an Israelite dedicated and that went out to a priest, and the priest consecrated it. That he may not say: Since it goes out to the priests at the Jubilee [it is mine]. For this priest who consecrates his dedicated field is as if he consecrated an ancestral field. And it is logical: just as an Israelite’s ancestral field that went out at the Jubilee, which one of the priests redeemed, goes out from under his hand and is divided among all the priests, as it says above in our chapter: “his ancestral possession,” his own, and this one is not his own, so too one who consecrates his dedicated field: it too is divided among his brothers the priests.]
gershom:a7.1: And the other: the Rabbis derive this from the [extra] heh of “haḥerem.”]
gershom:a8.1: He holds in accordance with Rabbi Yishmael: that is, he derives that it takes effect on offerings of the most sacred order and on offerings of lesser sanctity from where Rabbi Yishmael derives it, as we learned [in the mishna]: Rabbi Yishmael says: One verse says “you shall consecrate,” as it is written: “All the firstborn that is born… you shall consecrate,” and so on; and one verse says “do not consecrate,” as it is written: “However, the firstborn that is born first to the Lord among animals, a man shall not consecrate it.” How so? You consecrate it with a consecration of value, as we said: if it was a vow, he gives their value, and if a gift offering, he gives the benefit of discretion to Temple maintenance, which is a consecration of value for its worth; and you do not consecrate it with a consecration for the altar, for the sake of another offering. The Merciful One revealed this with offerings of lesser sanctity [such as a firstborn: that it takes effect on offerings of lesser sanctity], and the same is true of offerings of the most sacred order, that a dedication takes effect on them as a consecration of value, as we said.
gershom:a9.1: [The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: who said unspecified dedications are for Temple maintenance.
gershom:a10.1: The baraita is taught the opposite way: since it establishes that [opinion] of Rabbi Yehuda as that of the Rabbis.]
gershom:a11.1: He teaches the mishna the opposite way as well: since he teaches the baraita the opposite way.
gershom:a12.1: Rav learned it by tradition: for his teacher taught it to him [as] the baraita [has it], reversed.
gershom:a13.1: [If so: since he reversed [the opinion] of Rabbi Yehuda to be that of the Rabbis, he should have said the halakha is in accordance with the Rabbis.
gershom:a14.1: This is what he is saying: For me, this that I stated in the name of Rabbi Yehuda, I learned it in the name of the Rabbis; [but] for you, according to what you reversed and teach as Rabbi Yehuda’s, that [unspecified dedications are] for Temple maintenance, the halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.]
gershom:a15.1: And throw them into the river, and it will be permitted to you: because he holds unspecified dedications are for Temple maintenance, and since there is no Temple, there is no remedy except redemption and throwing [the money] into the river.
gershom:a16.1: [This applies when the Temple is standing: it would not be permitted to redeem it ab initio except at its value, because of the loss to the Temple treasury.]
gershom:a17.1: To publicize the matter that it is redeemed property: that is why he required four dinars, which are significant; but in any case a peruta suffices, as Shmuel [said].
gershom:a18.1: [I would have given all of it to the priests: evidently he holds unspecified dedications are for the priests, and since there are priests, priests’ dedications have no redemption.]
gershom:a19.1: Rabbi Shimon [says]: from here [we learn] that [the law of] dedicated fields is practiced only at a time when the Jubilee is in force, but movable property [is affected] even in the present time.
gershom:a20.1: A ger toshav is not practiced: that we are commanded to sustain him and are warned against wronging him. A ger toshav is one who renounces idol worship. And it is also written of a ger toshav: “Where it is well for him; you shall not wrong him,” for this “where it is well for him” is written in [the passage of] “You shall not deliver a slave to his master,” and the Sifrei explains: this is a ger toshav.
gershom:a21.1: [We learn from here that [the law of] dedicated fields is practiced only at a time when the Jubilee is in force; so why did Rav Yehuda require redemption? It is not difficult: land [is affected] only at a time when the Jubilee is in force, but movable property even in the present time.]
gershom:a22.1: But the incident in Pumbedita was also with land: for it says he dedicated all his property, both land and movable property.
gershom:a23.1: Land outside the Land [of Israel] is considered like movable property in the Land of Israel: and we said that with movable property it is practiced even in the present time.
gershom:a24.1: [A person may dedicate his sacrificial animals, and so on: as we explained above.] [Rabbeinu Gershom here cites the opening words of this part of the mishna on 28b.]
gershom:a25.1: Rabbi Yishmael says: One verse, and so on: for Rabbi Yishmael derives from these verses that it takes effect on offerings of the most sacred order and on offerings of lesser sanctity, as we explained above.
gershom:a26.1: And the Rabbis: who do not derive it from these verses, what do they need [these verses] for?
gershom:a27.1: [“Do not consecrate”: as it is written: “A man shall not consecrate it,” is needed to make him liable for a prohibition if he consecrates it for another offering.]
gershom:a28.1: “You shall consecrate” is needed: that it is a mitzva to consecrate it for the sake of a firstborn.
gershom:a29.1: And Rabbi Yishmael says to you: it is not needed for this, for a firstborn is consecrated on its own, as its sanctity is from the womb; rather, the verse comes only for what we said.
gershom:a30.1: And Rabbi Yishmael: that verse, “Every dedicated item is [most] sacred,” from which the Rabbis derive that it takes effect on offerings of the most sacred order [dedications for Temple maintenance, as it is stated: “Every dedicated item is most sacred”] and on offerings of lesser sanctity, what does he do with it? [This question and the answer in the next note are not in the printed Gemara.]
gershom:a31.1: Rabbi Yishmael holds in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who expounds that verse, “Every dedicated item is most sacred,” [to teach] that unspecified dedications are for Temple maintenance [as it is stated: “Every dedicated item is most sacred to the Lord”].
gershom:a32.1: We will return to you, [chapter] HaMakdish.
rashi:b1.1: Mishna. One who sells, at the time of the Jubilee: when the Jubilee is in force.
rashi:b1.2: Less than two years: but after two years, if he wishes to redeem it, he redeems it against the buyer’s will and gives him according to what he sold it for, as it is written: “Then let him count the years of its sale” (Leviticus 25:27). He calculates how many years there were from when he sold it until the Jubilee and divides the money according to the years. For example, if he sold it ten years before the Jubilee for ten litra, it emerges that he sold the produce of each year for a litra, for an unspecified sale is only until the Jubilee. Therefore, if it remained in the buyer’s hand five years and afterward the seller comes to redeem it, the buyer deducts five litra for him, a litra for each year that he consumed it, for that is how the reckoning came out at the start.
rashi:b2.1: Does not count toward the tally: of the two years, for it is written “years of crops”: two years fit for crops it must remain in the buyer’s hand. But if it was a year fit for crops and he plowed it and did not sow it, or left it fallow, that is, he left it uncultivated without even plowing it, he caused his own loss, and it counts for him toward the tally of the two years.
rashi:b2.2: Three crops: the one standing in it at the time of purchase, and two crops in the two years that it will be in his hand.
rashi:b3.1: Gemara. It does not teach “he does not redeem”: which would mean that it is not the law that the buyer is compelled to return it to him by redemption in less than two years.
rashi:b3.2: That even rattling is also prohibited: for the seller to show coins to the buyer so that he will be pleased to return it to him.
rashi:b4.1: “Years you shall buy”: “According to the number of years after the Jubilee you shall buy,” which means that it should be bought by him for two years; and if he returns it to him before that, he transgresses a positive mitzva.
rashi:b5.1: It is sold and goes out: at the Jubilee, and this buyer has lost his money.
rashi:b5.2: It is not sold at all: and the money is returned.
rashi:b6.1: A Hebrew maidservant goes out with the signs of young womanhood, as it is taught (Kiddushin 4a): “Then she shall go out for nothing”: these are the days of young womanhood.
rashi:b7.1: There: his daughter whom he sold in her minority and who went out free with the signs of young womanhood is never sold again, as we say (Kiddushin 18a): A person may not sell his daughter as a maidservant after [she was already] a maidservant, which we derive from “seeing he has dealt deceitfully with her”: once he has dealt deceitfully with her by selling her as a maidservant, he can no longer sell her. Therefore it is a complete going out, and one can say the a fortiori inference, that if he sells her in the days of young womanhood she is not sold. But a field that goes out to its owners at the Jubilee is sold again after the Jubilee if he wishes; therefore in the Jubilee Year, too, he may sell it, and it goes out to him for free.
rashi:b8.1: After the Jubilee: means immediately after the Jubilee.
rashi:b8.2: “Years you shall buy”: that if you buy a field, it shall be in your hand two years against the seller’s will, even if he wants to redeem it.
rashi:b8.3: According to the multitude of the years: that remain until the Jubilee, you shall increase its price: you shall sell it dearly, for it will be bought by him until the Jubilee if he does not redeem it. And according to the fewness of the years, you shall sell it cheaply, so that you do not wrong your fellow. And we learn from these verses that one may sell both close to the Jubilee that has passed and several years removed from it.
rashi:b9.1: For the number of years of crops: that it does not remain in the buyer’s hand at all, for in that very year [the owner] takes it from him; but it is sold to the extent that he loses his money.
rashi:b10.1: And we ask: “But if it is indeed sold”: after two years let him return it for free, on account of the Jubilee that passed over it. Isn’t it taught, and so on.
rashi:b10.2: He entered to consume it: for he began consuming it before the Jubilee; therefore we fulfill the verse for him, as it is written: “years of crops.” But one who buys in the Jubilee Year did not enter to consume it.
rashi:b11.1: One was this: that Shmuel said it is not sold at all.
rashi:b11.2: Goes out to freedom: for one who sells his slave to a gentile is penalized to redeem him and free him, because he removed him from mitzvot. And likewise one who sells his slave even to a Jew outside the Land: he goes out to freedom.
rashi:b12.1: In one, the sale is retracted: of these two, I heard from Master Shmuel that [in one] the sale is void and the money is returned: either in the case of one who sells his field in the Jubilee Year itself, or in the case of one who sells his slave to a Jew outside the Land.
rashi:b12.2: And in one, the sale is not retracted: rather, the buyer loses the money; and I do not know in which of them the sale is void. And if it is difficult: It is obvious that it is about one who sells his field in the Jubilee Year that Shmuel says the sale is void and the money is returned, for if the money is lost, what difference is there between Rav and Shmuel? There is a difference between them if the buyer went ahead and cut down trees that were in it. According to Rav, who said it is sold, the field returns, and the trees he cut, he has cut [and keeps]; according to Shmuel, who said it is not sold and the money is a gift, the trees are returned, even though the buyer does not take back money. Alternatively, such as where he sold movable property along with it, and the buyer took possession of the land [by an act of ḥazaka] and did not pull the movable property, for we hold (Kiddushin 26a): Property that does not serve as a guarantee is acquired along with property that serves as a guarantee by money, by a document or by ḥazaka, and does not require pulling. According to Rav, who said it is sold and goes out, the field returns and the movable property is acquired; according to Shmuel, who said it is not sold and the money is a gift, the movable property is not acquired, for the ḥazaka of the land is not a [valid] ḥazaka.
rashi:b13.1: Evidently the sale is not retracted: and the buyer loses. And since in that case we see that the sale is not retracted, certainly when Shmuel said in this case that it is not sold, [he meant that] the money is returned.
tosafot:b2.1: Mishna. If it was a year of blight or mildew, or the Sabbatical Year, it does not count toward the tally: In the chapter HaMekabel (Bava Metzia 106a) it explains that the blight and mildew were likewise throughout the world, for if the blight was [only] in the valley, in such a case we did not learn [here whether] it counts for him toward the tally. This is also precise, since it teaches it alongside the Sabbatical Year, when it is forbidden to sow (throughout the world).
tosafot:b2.2: If he plowed it or left it fallow, it counts toward the tally: The Gemara explains why it teaches “plowed”: since it teaches that “left it fallow” counts, all the more so “plowed.” And one could say: it teaches “not only this, but even this.”
tosafot:b7.1: There, she is not sold again: Rashi explained: His daughter whom he sold in her minority and who went out free with the signs of young womanhood is not sold again, as it says in Kiddushin (18a) that a person may not sell his daughter as a maidservant after [she was] a maidservant, as we derive from “seeing he has dealt deceitfully with her”: once he dealt deceitfully with her by selling her as a maidservant, he can no longer sell her; therefore it is a complete going out, and one can say the a fortiori inference. Thus far his words. But this does not seem right, for that is a dispute of tanna’im there. Therefore the Ri explained that even according to the one who says elsewhere that a person may sell his daughter as a maidservant after [she was] a maidservant, where she has at least brought signs [of young womanhood, he agrees that she is not sold]; so there is an a fortiori inference. However, it is somewhat difficult: with one who sells his field, too, it should follow from this a fortiori inference that it is not sold anymore. However, one can distinguish: it is not like the a fortiori inference of his daughter, since once the signs of young womanhood have come to her they will not leave her again; but with one who sells his field at the time of the Jubilee, the a fortiori inference is not as strong as with one who sells his daughter, for the Jubilee will pass and it will be as at the start. And one can also explain as Rashi explained, that a person may not sell his daughter as a maidservant after [she was] a maidservant; and although tanna’im disagree about it, we hold like Rabbi Shimon, who holds there that it is forbidden to sell [her again].
tosafot:b12.1: In brief: And I do not know in which of them the sale is void: Tosafot first quotes Rashi in full: it would seem obvious that the field sold in the Jubilee Year is the case where the sale is void and the money returned, for otherwise what would differ between Rav and Shmuel? There is a difference: trees the buyer cut down, or movable property sold along with the land and acquired through the buyer’s ḥazaka of the land (Kiddushin 26a); according to Rav the trees and the movable property stay with the buyer, and according to Shmuel they do not. Tosafot then raises the question people ask on Rashi’s view that the field is sold though it returns to its owner at once, and movable property is still acquired along with it: in the incident of Rabban Gamliel and the Elders on a ship (Bava Metzia 11a), he gave the tithe he would measure out to Rabbi Yehoshua and rented him its place, and the end of the account teaches that they received payment from one another. Why not give the place as a gift on condition that it be returned, or have it acquired by exchange [ḥalifin] with a cloth, or lend the place and have it acquired by a cloth? Tosafot answers: anything that returns to its owner, such as a gift on condition that it be returned, a loan or a rental, is not acquired by ḥalifin, since it is like a benefit of discretion, which (Bava Metzia 11b) is not money that can be acquired by ḥalifin; that is why they needed to receive payment from one another. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b1.1: [At the time of the Jubilee: when the Jubilee is in force.
gershom:b2.1: He is not permitted to redeem: his field from the buyer until after two years from its sale.
gershom:b3.1: As it is stated: “According to the number of years of the crops he shall sell to you”: that is, that it be in the buyer’s domain two years or more. And when he redeems it, he calculates the money that the buyer gave him for the field against the years from the time of sale until the Jubilee, and however much of the money comes to each year, so the buyer deducts for the seller according to the years it was in the buyer’s domain, as it is stated: “Then let him count the years of its sale,” that it was in the buyer’s domain, and according to them he deducts from the price of his redemption according to the reckoning of the price of the years, and the remainder of the money is returned to him, and he receives his field, as it is written: “And restore the surplus to the man to whom he sold it, and he shall return to his possession.”
gershom:b4.1: If those two years that it was in the buyer’s hand were a year of blight or mildew, when the grain did not grow, or if one of them was the Sabbatical Year,] it does not count for him toward the tally of the years of crops; rather, he must leave it further in his domain [until there are] two years fit for sowing and for crops. And what we said, that it does not count for him, applies only to an act of Heaven such as this; but if he was negligent with it [and did not sow] (that he plowed and did not sow, or left it fallow, that he did not plow and did not sow), it counts for him toward the tally of two years even though there were no crops in them, and the seller may redeem it immediately at the end of two years.
gershom:b5.1: [Rabbi Elazar says [the printed mishna reads Rabbi Eliezer]: Sometimes the buyer consumes three crops in two years. How so? If he sold it to him full of produce before Rosh HaShana, he consumes that standing produce, and at the end of this coming year another crop, and in the second year a third crop.
gershom:b6.1: Evidently: there is a prohibition too if he redeems it before the two years are complete, for] even rattling coins is prohibited; that is, the seller is forbidden even to show the coins set aside for the redemption, to show them to the buyer, during those two years that the Torah granted him, that it be in his domain.
gershom:b7.1: Even the buyer as well: if he persuades him to redeem it within those two years.
gershom:b8.1: Stands in violation of a positive mitzva: if he accepts the money.
gershom:b9.1: For we require “years you shall buy”: two full years, and there are not.
gershom:b10.1: Rav said it is sold: that the money is not returned.
gershom:b11.1: And goes out: that it returns to him at the Jubilee.
gershom:b12.1: Shmuel said it is not sold at all: that even the money is returned to him.
gershom:b13.1: That is not sold: that in the Jubilee Year it is not [considered] sold, since it returns to its owners; is it not logical that it is not sold at all, so that the money is returned?
gershom:b14.1: [And according to Rav, is there no a fortiori inference?] And according to Rav, do we not say an a fortiori inference in such a case? But isn’t it taught: One might have thought a person may sell, and so on. And what, if [a daughter] already sold when she is a minor goes out at the time of young womanhood (she is released by her signs), for she acquires herself with the signs,
gershom:b15.1: That is not sold: at the time of young womanhood, is it not logical that she is not sold, so that the money is returned? Evidently we say an a fortiori inference in such a case.
gershom:b16.1: There: with his daughter who is a young woman; for that reason we say an a fortiori inference that she is not sold at all.
gershom:b17.1: For she is not sold again: ever again, once she is a young woman.
gershom:b18.1: Here: with one who sells his field in the Jubilee Year, since after the Jubilee it can be sold again in a complete sale, for that reason in the Jubilee Year [too] it is sold and goes out, and the money is not returned, and we do not say an a fortiori inference [here].
gershom:b19.1: “After the Jubilee… years you shall buy”: that is what is written: “According to the number of years after the Jubilee you shall buy.”
gershom:b20.1: Teaches that one may sell: immediately, right after [the Jubilee has passed], for years of crops, for two years.
gershom:b21.1: Separated from the Jubilee, from where: that one may also sell far from the Jubilee, such as ten years [after the Jubilee] or twenty years after the Jubilee.
gershom:b22.1: The verse states: “According to the multitude of the years [and according to the fewness of the years]”: “according to the multitude of the years” is where he sold it close to the [previous] Jubilee, so that he still has many years until the Jubilee.
gershom:b23.1: And according to the fewness of the years: that is, he sold it far from the Jubilee, so that only a few years remain until the Jubilee [Year].
gershom:b24.1: [Rav could say to you: it is not sold: in the Jubilee Year, with regard to the number of years of crops, that the buyer could hold it for two years.
gershom:b25.1: But it is sold: in that the sale is not retracted, and it goes out at the Jubilee.
gershom:b26.1: But if it is indeed sold: as you say, that the money is not returned, let those coins that the buyer gave be a purchase for him, that it stand in his domain until after the Jubilee; and after the Jubilee let him consume [it for] years of crops and return it without money, just as it would go out at the Jubilee without money.]
gershom:b27.1: Isn’t it taught: [If he sold it to him one year before the Jubilee and he consumed it one year before the Jubilee, one completes for him a second year, another one, after the Jubilee]; evidently the Jubilee does not cancel his sale.
gershom:b28.1: [There, he entered to consume: since he already consumed it one year before the Jubilee, therefore one completes it for him after the Jubilee.
gershom:b29.1: Here: where he sold it in the Jubilee Year, he did not enter to consume anything before the Jubilee; therefore he cannot consume the number of years of crops after the Jubilee, but it is sold and goes out.
gershom:b30.1: One was this: Shmuel said it is not sold.
gershom:b31.1: One who sells his slave to a gentile: one penalizes his master to redeem him, and he goes out to freedom.
gershom:b32.1: Or if he sold him to a Jew outside the Land: one penalizes the buyer, and he goes out to freedom.
gershom:b33.1: In one the sale is retracted: the money [is returned] to the buyer.
gershom:b34.1: Since it teaches that he goes out to freedom and requires a bill of manumission from his second master,] conclude from it that his second master acquired him and the sale is not retracted [so as to return] the money to the buyer; for if the sale were retracted, he would not need a bill from his second master but from his first master. [And Rav Anan, who said: I do not know in which of them the sale is retracted.] [The last words begin the Gemara’s next question, on 30a.]
